body:
A satellite is more than its main instrument

An artificial satellite is a complete working system. Its scientific or service instruments must receive electrical power, maintain the correct direction, communicate with Earth and survive the conditions of space.

A useful basic distinction is between the payload and the satellite bus, also called the spacecraft platform.

The payload is the equipment that performs the satellite's principal mission. The satellite bus comprises the supporting systems that allow the payload and spacecraft to operate, such as power supply, communication, control, structure and thermal protection.

Payload: the equipment that performs the mission

The payload depends on why the satellite was built.

  • Earth-observation satellite: Its payload may include cameras or other sensors that collect information about Earth's surface.
  • Communication satellite: Its payload may include transponders, which receive communication signals and retransmit them to other locations.
  • Weather satellite: Its payload may include instruments that observe clouds, atmospheric conditions and weather systems.
  • Navigation satellite: Its payload transmits precisely timed navigation signals that receivers can use for positioning and timing.

The payload answers the question, What work is this satellite intended to perform? The spacecraft's supporting systems answer the question, What keeps that work possible?

Power system: supplying electricity in space

Satellites need electricity for their computers, instruments, transmitters, receivers and other equipment.

Many Earth-orbiting satellites use solar arrays to convert sunlight into electrical energy. They also use rechargeable batteries to store electrical energy.

When a satellite passes through Earth's shadow, its solar arrays may no longer receive direct sunlight. During this period, the batteries can supply electrical power. When sunlight is available again, the power system can operate the spacecraft and recharge the batteries.

This distinction is essential: solar arrays generate electricity from sunlight, whereas batteries store electrical energy for later use.

ISRO's GSAT-16 communication satellite provides a documented Indian example of a spacecraft equipped with solar arrays and rechargeable lithium-ion batteries. The example illustrates a general principle; it does not mean all satellites have identical power arrangements.

Communication system: exchanging information with Earth

A satellite uses antennas, transmitters and receivers to exchange signals with ground stations or other users. Radio communication makes it possible to send instructions to the satellite and receive information from it.

Two important kinds of communication must be distinguished:

  • Mission-control communication: Ground controllers send commands and receive information about the satellite's operation.
  • Payload communication: The satellite sends the observations, signals or communication services for which its mission was designed.

For example, an imaging satellite may send a photograph of Earth's surface as payload data. It may separately send its battery status, temperature and other operating information as telemetry. These are different types of information, even when related communication equipment is used.

Attitude control and orbit control

A satellite often needs to point its instruments accurately. A camera may need to face Earth, a solar array may need suitable exposure to sunlight, and an antenna may need to face a ground station.

The direction in which the satellite is pointing is called its attitude. Its position and path around Earth describe its orbit.

Attitude control manages the spacecraft's orientation. Orbit control adjusts its orbital path when necessary. These are related but distinct functions.

Small onboard actuators and propulsion systems can help a spacecraft maintain orientation or make occasional orbital corrections. A satellite in orbit does not need continuous engine firing to overcome gravity.

Other essential supporting systems

  • Onboard computer: Coordinates spacecraft functions, processes instructions and manages operating tasks.
  • Thermal control: Helps keep equipment within suitable temperature limits despite heating by sunlight and cooling in shadow.
  • Structure: Supports the instruments and other spacecraft components and withstands the conditions of launch and operation.
  • Propulsion, where provided: Performs selected orbital adjustments and manoeuvres.

Satellite operation and working life

A satellite may function for years, but its useful life is not unlimited. Batteries and other components can degrade, equipment can fail, and a spacecraft may eventually lack the propellant needed for important corrections.

The practical working life of a satellite depends on its design, the space environment, the condition of its subsystems and the requirements of its mission.

Prelims focus

  • Payload means the satellite equipment that performs its principal mission.
  • The satellite bus provides supporting functions such as power, control and communication.
  • Solar arrays generate electricity; batteries store electrical energy.
  • Telemetry reports spacecraft operating conditions, while payload data represents the mission's observations or services.
  • Attitude describes the direction a spacecraft points; orbit describes its path around Earth.
  • Trap: A satellite's camera or transponder is not the same as its solar array or supporting power system.

[Sources: Indian Space Research Organisation, 'GSAT-16', sections 'Power', 'Payloads of GSAT-16' and mission description; consulted 4 November 2026. Indian Space Research Organisation, 'Space Applications Centre (SAC)', descriptions of communication transponders and optical and microwave sensors; consulted 4 November 2026. Indian Space Research Organisation, 'AstroSat – Ground Segment', sections 'TTC and Payload Data Reception Station' and 'Satellite Control Centre'; consulted 4 November 2026. NCERT, Science, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Chapter 12, 'Electricity and Circuits', pp. 116–121.]

body:
Why does a satellite need a ground segment?

A satellite may carry advanced instruments, but its mission also requires facilities on Earth. These facilities help operate the spacecraft, receive information from it and turn that information into a useful service or product.

The ground segment includes ground stations, antennas, control centres, communication links and data-processing facilities used to support a satellite mission.

A satellite and its ground facilities therefore form parts of one operating system. The spacecraft works in space, while the ground segment supports its operation and helps deliver useful information to users.

Tracking, telemetry and command

Three basic functions are commonly grouped as TT&C: Tracking, Telemetry and Command.

Tracking

Tracking involves determining the satellite's position and motion. Ground facilities use received signals and other measurements to follow the spacecraft and help calculate or verify its orbit.

Telemetry

Telemetry means information sent from the satellite to the ground about its condition and operation. Examples include battery status, equipment temperatures and the functioning of important onboard systems.

Telemetry helps controllers identify whether the spacecraft is functioning normally and whether corrective action may be necessary.

Command or telecommand

A telecommand is an instruction sent from a ground-control facility to a satellite. Controllers may command the spacecraft to activate an instrument, change an operating mode or perform a planned manoeuvre.

The direction of communication is important:

  • Uplink: A signal travels from Earth towards the satellite.
  • Downlink: A signal travels from the satellite towards Earth.

Commands are normally sent by uplink. Telemetry and mission data are normally received by downlink.

Tracking tells controllers where the spacecraft is. Telemetry tells them how it is functioning. Telecommand allows them to instruct it.

How information reaches the user

Consider an Earth-observation satellite carrying a camera. The camera collects information about Earth's surface. The satellite transmits the observations to a receiving facility when communication is available. Ground systems process the information into images or other useful products that can be examined by intended users.

Such data may support the study of agricultural conditions, land use, coastal changes or flooding. For a region in Gujarat, for example, satellite observations can provide information useful for studying changes in agricultural land or the coastline.

This is distinct from the operation of a communication satellite. A communication payload can receive a signal sent from one ground location and relay it towards another receiving location. In both cases, the satellite and the equipment on Earth perform different parts of the service.

India's main facilities relevant to satellite operation

Several organisations within the Indian Space Research Organisation perform different functions in launching, developing and operating spacecraft.

FacilityLocationMain function
SDSC SHARSriharikota, Andhra PradeshLaunch-base infrastructure and launch operations.
ISTRACBengaluru, KarnatakaTracking, telemetry, command and mission-operation support through a network of stations.
MCFHassan, Karnataka, and Bhopal, Madhya PradeshMonitoring and controlling ISRO's geostationary and geosynchronous satellites.
SACAhmedabad, GujaratDevelopment of satellite payloads and applications, including communication transponders and remote-sensing instruments.

ISTRAC: tracking and mission support

The ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC), headquartered in Bengaluru, provides tracking support for satellite and launch-vehicle missions. It also supports mission operations for remote-sensing and scientific satellites.

Its network of ground facilities allows signals to be exchanged with spacecraft when they are within suitable communication range. Ground systems help determine spacecraft position, monitor operating conditions and transmit commands.

MCF: controlling geostationary and geosynchronous satellites

The Master Control Facility (MCF) operates from Hassan and Bhopal. It monitors and controls geostationary and geosynchronous satellites belonging to ISRO's satellite systems.

Its responsibilities include initial orbit-raising operations, monitoring spacecraft health and carrying out necessary station-keeping activities. Station-keeping means making occasional corrections to maintain a satellite within its required orbital region or operating position.

This is especially relevant for GEO satellites because their mission often depends on remaining near a designated longitude.

SAC: Gujarat's direct connection with satellite technology

The Space Applications Centre (SAC) is located in Ahmedabad, Gujarat. It develops spacecraft instruments and technologies used for communication, navigation and Earth observation.

SAC's work includes communication transponders for Indian communication satellites and optical and microwave sensors for Earth-observation missions. Its activities also extend to processing and applying satellite-derived information.

Examples of relevant application areas include agriculture, environmental monitoring, geosciences, climate studies and ocean-related observations.

The distinction between SAC and SDSC SHAR is important: SAC in Ahmedabad develops payloads and applications; SDSC SHAR at Sriharikota provides launch infrastructure.

Connecting all the concepts

A complete satellite mission connects the ideas studied in this lesson. First, a launch vehicle uses propulsion systems and stages to give a satellite the required motion. The selected orbit determines how the spacecraft travels and what parts of Earth it can observe or serve. The satellite's payload performs the intended work, while its power, control and communication systems keep it operating. Finally, the ground segment manages the spacecraft and receives or relays information for users.

The most suitable orbit depends on the work required. A low polar or Sun-synchronous orbit may help observe changing conditions over many regions. MEO is common for large navigation constellations. GEO is useful when continuous observation or communication over a particular broad region is required. These uses depend on mission requirements rather than on a rigid rule that each orbit performs only 1 function.

Prelims focus

  • TT&C stands for Tracking, Telemetry and Command.
  • Uplink means Earth to satellite; downlink means satellite to Earth.
  • Telemetry concerns satellite health and operation; payload data concerns the mission's observations or services.
  • ISTRAC is headquartered in Bengaluru; MCF operates from Hassan and Bhopal.
  • Space Applications Centre is located in Ahmedabad, Gujarat.
  • Trap: SAC develops payloads and applications; it is not India's principal rocket launch centre.

[Sources: Indian Space Research Organisation, 'ISRO Telemetry, Tracking and Command Network (ISTRAC)', centre overview and objectives; 'Ground Segment Activities', sections 'MCF' and 'SAC'; 'Space Applications Centre (SAC)', centre overview; 'Satish Dhawan Space Centre (SDSC) SHAR', centre overview; 'AstroSat – Ground Segment', sections 'TTC and Payload Data Reception Station', 'Satellite Control Centre' and 'Mission Operations'; all consulted 4 November 2026. European Space Agency, 'Types of orbits', sections 'Low Earth orbit (LEO)', 'Medium Earth orbit (MEO)', 'Polar orbit (PO)', 'Sun synchronous orbit (SSO)' and 'Geostationary orbit (GEO)', published 30 March 2020; consulted 4 November 2026.]
